## Handoff / reflection (day 345)
Title: "Luncheonette, Four O'Clock". Signed "C.L" small in the street at the lower right (sig pile: sienna/red earth/black, round 1.1).
This sitting (days 198–345): relettered the sign with proper spacing; deepened the curtains; added coffee urns, a brass rod and a cake stand so the shop windows read as a lunch room; trimmed the counterman's silhouette; repainted the shaded sidewalk as a two-pile gradient; repainted the whole sky to get rid of the rectangle behind the tower; repainted the woman in the open window with sloped shoulders, a sleeve and forearms crossed on the sill; and closed the lower sashes of three windows so the window pattern is less regular.
Judgments on the passages left open last time:
- Poster-flat surfaces: ACCEPTED as the picture's manner.
- Shaded sidewalk and street uniform: IMPROVED (the sidewalk now runs from deep at the wall to lighter at the curb). The street strip is ACCEPTED as it is: it's a thin band.
- Schematic shop glass: IMPROVED with objects. The bands remain, and I accept them.
- Lamppost shadow: ACCEPTED (the big shadow edge comes from a roofline, so it doesn't need to converge).
- Sky rectangle: SOLVED by repainting the whole field.
Still uncertain: the woman's forearms are a simple band. They're legible at viewing distance, but she isn't really modelled.
Practical lessons (hypotheses tested so far):
- To correct a flat field, repaint the WHOLE field bounded by real edges, with a gradient of piles if needed (work piles=, coverage 3, fill, clip, over DRY). It left no seams on the sky or the sidewalk. Broken scumbles failed.
- Before an exclusion repaint, grow the masks 0.8 around the thin dark shapes. Then do a second small-brush pass along any receding diagonal edge, which the broad pass misses.
- Pale over dark needs DRY dark. Dark over pale (trimming a silhouette) covers in one coat of glass dark over dry paint.
- A new hand-lettered sign needs per-glyph widths and optical gaps (LW/LG + layout()); equal pitch gave ragged spacing.
- Small figures: paint out the old silhouette with background dark, wait until dry, then lay the new masks in lit/mid/shade vertical splits.
- Drying times: earth/black details 10–20 days, lead-white fields 3–8 days at medium 0.08.

I've finished **Luncheonette, Four O'Clock**.

It's a red-brick corner building in low afternoon sun. The shadow of a building outside the picture cuts diagonally across the lower left of the front wall and the sidewalk. A counterman in a white coat stands in the dark doorway under the green LUNCHEONETTE sign. Above him and a little to the left, a woman rests her crossed forearms on the sill of the one open window, and neither knows the other is there. A lamppost, pale buildings farther off with a water tower, and a clear sky make the quiet right-hand side.

**What I did this sitting (painting clock day 198 to day 345):**
- **Sign:** I repainted the lettering. Each letter now has its own width and spacing, so the word reads evenly.
- **Shop windows:** I darkened the curtains from paper-white to cream, so the light looks like it's coming through glass. I added two coffee urns, a brass curtain rod and a cake stand under a glass dome, so the windows now read as a lunch room.
- **Figures:** I darkened a light sliver beside the counterman's arm. I painted the woman again with sloped shoulders, a sleeve and crossed forearms.
- **Windows above:** I closed the lower half of three windows so the pattern of open and shut panes is less regular.
- **Sidewalk:** I repainted the whole shaded part as a gradient, from deep at the wall to lighter toward the curb.
- **Sky:** I repainted the whole sky, which removed the faint rectangle behind the water tower.
- I signed it small in the street at the lower right.

**How I judged last time's open problems:**
- **Faint rectangle in the sky:** gone.

I looked again at the whole canvas in normal colour, then in value and squint together. The counterman in the dark doorway is still where the eye goes first, and the lit sidewalk, the storefront and the pale distant blocks carry the light. Nothing in the big shapes is weak.
Passages left open before, checked in detail crops:
- The woman in the open window (crop 380–520 × 130–250): the crossed forearms read and her shoulders slope. ACCEPTED. At about 45 units tall, more modelling would get fussy.
- The open window's raised sash: the greyer left end of the blind band and two tiny dark dashes on the sash rail look like the shaded inside of the open frame. ACCEPTED.
- The counterman's hem and silhouette (crop 420–560 × 400–580): clean, and the hem reads as turned up. A couple of tiny pale flecks at his left shoulder can't be seen at viewing distance. ACCEPTED.
- Shaded brick close in value to the lit brick: ACCEPTED as before. In the squint view the diagonal shadow still reads, carried by the storefront and the sidewalk.
- Specks in the distant shop bands and the poster-flat surfaces: ACCEPTED as before.
No paint this sitting. Any further touch would add risk without improving the picture.
Handoff lessons carried forward (hypotheses where noted): repaint whole fields up to real edges (work piles=, coverage 3, fill, clip, over DRY paint); pale over DRY dark only; broken scumbles read as spots on these flat fields; restate small areas with the exact original pile and stop at a real edge; hand lettering needs a width per letter and optical gaps; drying takes 10–20 days for earth/black details and 3–8 days for lead-white fields at medium .08.
Finished. Heart happy: yes.

I'm leaving **Luncheonette, Four O'Clock** finished as it is. I didn't add any paint this sitting.

It's a red-brick corner building in low four-o'clock sun. The shadow of a building outside the picture cuts diagonally across the lower left of the front wall and the sidewalk. A counterman in a white coat stands in the dark doorway under the green LUNCHEONETTE sign. Above him and a little to the left, a woman rests her folded arms on the sill of the one open window, and neither knows the other is there. The lamppost, the water tower and the pale buildings farther off make the quiet right side.

I looked at the whole canvas again in normal colour, then in grey values and squinting. The picture still holds, and the white coat in the dark doorway is where the eye goes first. Then I checked each passage I had left open, in close-up:
- **The woman:** her crossed forearms and sloping shoulders read clearly. I'm leaving her as she is, because she's so small that more modelling would look fussy.
- **Her window:** a greyer patch at one end of the raised sash looks like the shaded inside of the open frame.
- **The counterman:** his hem and outline are clean. A couple of tiny pale flecks at his shoulder can't be seen at viewing distance.
- **The shaded brick:** it's still close in value to the sunlit brick. I'm leaving it, because the shadow across the storefront and sidewalk makes the cast shadow read.
- **Leftovers I'm also accepting:** the specks in the distant shopfronts and the flat, poster-like surfaces.

**Practical lessons (also in the journal):**
- To fix a flat area, repaint the whole of it up to real edges, over dry paint.
- Pale paint goes over a dark only when the dark is fully dry.
- Thin broken layers of paint look like spots on these flat surfaces.
- Small touch-ups need the exact original mix and should stop at a real edge.
- Hand-lettering needs a width for each letter and adjusted gaps between them.
- Drying times:
  - Small details in earth colours and black: about 10–20 days.
  - Areas mixed mostly from lead white: about 3–8 days.

My heart is happy with it. It's a quiet, sunlit corner with two people alone at four o'clock.
